To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Puerto Rican OEF/OIF women veterans were younger, more likely to be Hispanic, and less likely to be married than the U.S. women veterans; had higher rates of mental health conditions and physical health conditions; and used VA health care at lower rates.

1) Puerto Rican OEF/OIF women Veterans had a higher prevalence of mental health disorders and a lower prevalence of physical health problems compared with their US counterparts; 2) Puerto Rican OIF/OEF women Veterans used fewer VA services compared with their US peers, and 3) Puerto Rican women Veterans had a lower rate of service utilization than US OEF/OIF Veterans.

Puerto Rico women veterans have more severe physical and mental health problems, are younger than women veterans in the US, have higher rates of VA health care utilization, and are less likely to be married than US women veterans.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the health of women veterans, and in particular with the health of OIF/OEF women veterans, and with the health services they use.
the physical and mental health profiles and health care utilization patterns of Operation Iraqi Freedom/ Operation Enduring Freedom women veterans in Puerto Rico versus those in the United States.
the health and health care of women who have served in the military during the post-9/11 wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there are significant differences in the mental and physical health profiles of female Veterans in Puerto Rico and the US, and the differences are not explained by the fact that the women in Puerto Rico are older.

there is a lack of evidence to suggest that the current system in Puerto Rico is failing women veterans in terms of physical and mental health outcomes, or that they are using VA health services at higher rates than women veterans in the continental United States (CONUS) (see Figure 1 for the study design).
the VA has not done a very good job at serving female veterans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Puerto Rican women Veterans have a different profile of health care utilization and health conditions than women Veterans from the mainland.

there are differences between women veterans in PR and the US, but that these differences are not necessarily a function of their Puerto Rican heritage, but of the unique characteristics of the women veterans in PR.
the VA has a large population of female veterans in Puerto Rico that are not receiving the services that they need.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are differences between women veterans who live in Puerto Rico and those who live in the United States.
there is a need to improve our understanding of the health needs and utilization patterns of OIF/OEF female veterans, and to develop and implement effective strategies to meet those needs.
women Veterans who served in Iraq and Afghanistan are more likely to be diagnosed with PTSD and depression and to have higher rates of suicide ideation than other women Veterans.
